A B S T R A C T
Accurate measurement of lower-limb joint angles is essential for gait analysis, rehabilitation, and early
detection of degenerative disease. Current marker-based approaches using wearable sensors not only require
complex setups but also intricate calibrations, hindering widespread application of them in daily life. This
study aimed to propose a vision-based estimation of hip, knee, and ankle angles directly from single-view RGB
frames. An end-to-end model that integrated a convolutional neural network for spatial feature extraction
with a transformer module to capture temporal gait dynamics was built, and a novel loss function that jointly
penalizes angle and angular-velocity errors improved overall consistency and accuracy of the estimation. The
performance of the developed model was compared with that of the 3D pose method, and its robustness was
examined by varying camera perspectives, walking speeds, and abnormality in gait patterns. The proposed
model achieved the intraclass correlation coefficients above 0.92 across varying viewing angles, walking
speeds, and gait patterns. The model outperformed the two-stage baseline of the 3D pose method. The proposed
model not only eliminates the need for complex setups and sensors but is also less prone to inaccuracies
compared to the two-stage pipeline method. When applied to clinical and home-based environments, it can
offer a cost-effective and reliable solution for gait assessment.

tems use multiple cameras and body markers to deliver accurate joint
angle data and are regarded as the gold standard. Wearable sensors,
such as inertial measurement units (IMUs) and surface electromyog-
raphy (sEMG) sensors, are attached directly to the body to capture

regarding setups and user discomfort. The setups for MoCap often

ing discrepancies between the estimated and actual joint centers. These

subsequent 2D-to-3D pose reconstruction, amplifying inaccuracies, un-
derscoring the need for robust single-camera solutions that generalize
well across diverse populations and recording conditions.
These challenges further limit the applicability of pose estimation
models in clinical and real-world environments. Studies have demon-
strated that achieving accuracy comparable to clinical standards often
requires vision-based systems to employ multi-view camera setups to
resolve occlusions and ensure 3D fidelity [14]. Thus, it necessitates
synchronized hardware and dedicated capture spaces akin to tradi-
tional laboratory settings. To overcome the challenge, single-camera
approaches have been proposed, offering greater accessibility, but they
rely on the explicit knowledge of intrinsic camera parameters or require
specific calibration objects in the scene to recover absolute scale [15].
These impede the widespread adoption of markerless pose estimation
technologies for remote monitoring scenarios, where non-expert users
typically rely on uncalibrated consumer devices without any assistance
from trained professionals.

Building on this motivation, we propose an end-to-end model that
can estimate lower-limb joint angles directly from video frames col-
lected from a single RGB camera, eliminating the two-stage pipeline of
the 3D pose method. The model will leverage a combination of spatial
feature extraction and temporal modeling, and its performance will be
validated across varying camera viewpoints, walking speeds, and gait
patterns. The contributions of this study include:
1. a robust, single-camera joint angle estimation model that can be
generalized across various viewpoints, walking speeds, and gait
patterns,
2. an end-to-end deep learning architecture integrating both spatial
and temporal modeling,
3. enriched gait analysis that can benefit from precise prediction of
joint angles and angular velocities,
4. a comprehensive joint angle dataset developed not only for joint
angle estimation but also for early identification of diseases.

2.5. Loss function
Our model was trained using a multi-task loss that jointly optimized

applied to the input construction. Each joint angle was normalized to
fall within the interval of 0 and 1 by its range of motion. To obtain the
ground truth for the joint angular velocity ground truth, the difference

the knees exhibit distinct and high-amplitude flexion-extension patterns
that provide strong visual cues, allowing the spatial feature extractor to
capture their dynamics with greater precision. A novel multi-task loss
function that jointly optimizes angle and angular-velocity predictions
contributed to improved overall consistency, as well.
The loss function used in this study was formulated to jointly
optimize the estimation of joint angles and their corresponding angu-
lar velocities. The model was trained using a multi-task loss, where
L1 losses were employed for both joint angle and angular velocity
predictions. In addition, a consistency loss term was incorporated to
promote temporal coherence by encouraging the predicted velocities to
match the finite differences of the predicted joint angles. This approach
allowed the model to take advantage of the inherent relationship
between angle and angular velocity, thereby improving both the ac-
curacy and temporal consistency of the predictions. Including angular
velocity in both the output and the loss calculation contributed to
overall performance gains. Notably, the inclusion of velocity prediction
improved the ICC from 0.9193 to 0.9285. Although the improvement
is modest, it indicates enhanced agreement with the ground truth and
highlights the value of incorporating dynamic features. This suggests
that leveraging both static and dynamic gait features during training
leads to more reliable estimation of lower-limb joint angles from video
data. This approach reflects recent trends in physics-aware motion
capture as well as state-of-the-art motion representation learning. It
has been demonstrated that the integration of velocity-level supervision
into the MotionBERT loss function has been shown to be crucial for
recovering smooth and temporally coherent 3D motion from partially
observed observations [26]. Studies nowadays have adopted explicit
physics-based learning strategies to enforce biological plausibility, uti-
lizing derivative-based constraints to eliminate physically impossible
artifacts [29.30].
This study explored several models as backbones for model devel
opment, and RegNetY was finally selected. Although all the backbone
models exhibited fairly strong performance, supporting the effective-
ness of the proposed model design, RegNetY provided the most robust
and consistent performance for both joint angle and angular velocity
among other backbone models. It can be speculated that the flexible
and scalable architecture of RegNetY is attributed to balancing depth,
width, and group convolution efficiently, enhancing feature represen
tation. The observation is supported by recent studies demonstrating
the strong feature extraction capabilities and efficiency of RegNet
architectures [23]. The developed model using RegNetY showed strong
performance in estimating lower limb joint angles, with the highest
accuracy for the knee. Incorporating angular velocity into the model
further improved prediction accuracy, suggesting the value of dynamic
features in prediction. Future quantization of the RegNetY backbone us
ing regression-specialized quantization methods such as Reg-PTQ [31]
and a quantized Transformer module such as Q-ViT [32] will minimize
the memory footprint and improve the applicability of the proposed
model.

The performance comparison between the developed model and the
3D pose model suggests that the developed model can be a reliable al-
ternative to it. The 3D pose approach relies on extracting 2D keypoints
from RGB images to be used in a lifting model that estimates 3D joint
positions. From these positions, joint angles are calculated [9–13]. Yet,
this process is rather prone to errors since the initial 2D keypoint local
ization can lead to compounded inaccuracies in the final estimates. By
contrast, the developed model achieved estimation closer to the ground
truth by estimating joint angles directly from video frames. Thus, the
risk of error propagation was reduced, especially during rapid phases
of gait for both timing and amplitude. This direct estimation not only
improves accuracy but also simplifies the workflow, making it a more
accessible alternative in gait analysis under various circumstances.
The developed model exhibited strong robustness to various sources
of variation, such as camera views, walking speeds, gait abnormalities,
and varying clothing conditions. The estimation across varying camera
views remained consistent, with only minor fluctuations in ICCs and
MAEs by views. Fair performance was once again confirmed with speed
variations. The prediction under both the usual and faster-than-usual
speed conditions closely matched ground truth trajectories, despite a
small deviation in mid-swing at faster-than-usual speed. The phase lag
observed at higher walking speeds might have derived from increased
motion blur of fast-moving distal joints, which degraded joint-related
spatial features and affected temporal estimation. The robustness of the
developed model in differentiating the gaits of sarcopenia patients and
Parkinson’s disease patients from normal ones further expanded the
potential scope of its application. This robustness extends to clothing
variations, as the model successfully inferred joint kinematics despite
loose pants obscuring the limbs by leveraging global body dynamics
and temporal patterns rather than relying solely on local joint visibility.
This robustness can be attributed to the end-to-end architecture of the
model, which combined powerful spatial feature extraction from each
video frame with temporal modeling using Transformers. By learning
both frame-level visual cues and their temporal relationships, the model
effectively captured essential gait dynamics, allowing it to maintain
performance across diverse conditions. This capability is critical for
real-world applications, where variability in recording settings and
patient conditions is common.
When the impact of input resolution on model performance was
investigated, it was found that reducing image resolutions led to only
a subtle degradation in accuracy, while high reliability was preserved
even at lower resolutions. This suggests that the proposed model effec-
tively captures global spatiotemporal gait patterns rather than relying
solely on fine-grained spatial details. This enhances the applicability
of the proposed model to real-world scenarios, where computational
resources or input quality may be limited. In particular, it supports
deployment in practical gait assessment settings that require both
robustness and efficiency.

strong feasibility for real-time gait analysis. The proposed model pro
cessed a video consisting of 1127 frames in 4.14 s, corresponding to
an average throughput of approximately 270 FPS, or about 3.7 ms per

monitoring of disease progression. Finally, its capability to quantify
dynamic gait features provides opportunities for the development of
scalable, video-based digital biomarkers to support future diagnostic

strategies, such as test-time augmentation and domain adaptation, can
be considered. Test-time augmentation, where multiple augmented
versions of the input are evaluated and aggregated, will improve the
robustness of the prediction. Domain adaptation techniques can be
applied to mitigate the domain gap between the training data and
real-world scenarios.

only a single participant was present in the frame. The performance of
the model in frames involving multiple individuals or in environments
where occlusions caused by daily life objects, such as furniture or
walking aids, is subject to further investigation. Second, the data were
collected in a controlled indoor setup where consistent lighting and
background were guaranteed.
5. Conclusion
This study developed and validated an end-to-end vision-based
model that can estimate lower-limb joint angles directly from video
frames. Using RegNetY as a backbone, the developed model integrated
a convolutional neural network for spatial feature extraction with a
transformer module to capture temporal gait dynamics. A novel loss
function that jointly penalizes angle and angular-velocity errors im-
proved overall estimation accuracy. The developed model exhibited
higher accuracy than the 3D pose model, achieving the highest ICC of
0.9652. The robustness of the developed model was confirmed across
varying camera views, speed conditions, and gait patterns. The devel-
oped model can usher in a more reliable and accessible gait assessment
in both clinical and home-based circumstances.
